criteria.note: docs/tracker-operator-guide.md is a HUMAN-FACING operator guide, not a second capability dump. It walks a person through the whole workflow in narrative sections ('Who this is for', 'What "wired" means before you start', 'Getting work IN: intake', 'What happens to the ticket AFTER: the round-trip', 'A full round-trip, walked through once', 'What you do, and what WARP does'), written in the second person for someone who never opens the repository. It is discoverable four ways: the README 'Tracker integration' bullet now links it as the day-to-day operator workflow; the README 'Repository contents' list gained a dedicated bullet; docs/plugin.md section 12 opening paragraph links it as the operator companion; and docs/manifest.yaml registers it (reading_order 6, WARP_Tracker_Operator_Guide.pdf). It defers the capability reference to section 12 and capabilities.yaml rather than restating it.

Intake is explained from the human's side. The routing signal is a label (concrete example warp-repo:web-app) with a Jira component and a named field named as the two alternatives - matching .warp/tracker.py MECHANISMS = ('label','component','field'). For Confluence it points to the shipped requirements template (plugin/templates/confluence-requirements-template.md) and its Outcomes / Acceptance Criteria / Open Decisions sections, all of which exist in that file. Intake is run via the /warp:intake skill (plugin/skills/intake/SKILL.md exists). What WARP produces is stated as a routing-resolved warp.spec/v1 DRAFT the human completes: for a bug AC1 is the reproduction written as a failing test plus a no-regression ACn; for a requirements page the ACs come from the page (AC1..ACn) plus the no-regression criterion; the source is linked in intake_source. It states intake FAILS CLOSED by name on a missing, unknown, or ambiguous signal and never falls back to a default - matching resolve_repo (TrackerRoutingError) and draft_spec_from_item/draft_spec_from_requirements (IntakeError).

The round-trip is stated plainly and correctly. The human does NOT hand-update the ticket: a one-way mirror driven by the event stream (never polling) transitions the issue and posts a closing comment. The event-to-status table (marked ready -> ready, blocked -> blocked, a review verdict recorded -> in_review, shipped -> shipped plus closing comment, merged -> merged) matches EVENT_STATUS in .warp/tracker_mirror.py exactly. Transitions use the human's OWN statuses through the per-org status_map (the JSON example matches plugin/templates/.warp/trackers.json), an unmapped WARP status is a comment not an invented transition, and omitting the status_map is comment-only - all matching resolve_status_map and the NG4 guarantee. A plan mirrors onto an epic (keyed to the plan, never forked) with a child per work item and a shipped rollup - matching tracker_epic_mirror. It is one-way, idempotent, never polls, the repository is the single source of truth and wins any disagreement, and an unwired spec is skipped by name.

Setup is actionable and true. The per-org .warp/trackers.json (routing plus status_map, template at plugin/templates/.warp/trackers.json) exists; the optional tracker_repo front-matter field is enforced in .warp/validate.py (tracker_routing_enforcement, fails closed against a wired config on an unknown repo, single-repo default when absent); auth is by reference token_ref with the example env:JIRA_TOKEN - the correct env-resolving example, not the template's non-resolving secrets:jira_token - resolved from a secrets store, never a raw credential in a file, prompt, proof, or log, failing closed if none resolves. The connection is described only as plain non-LLM Python that runs unattended and deterministically. The mechanical-versus-reference honesty is preserved: routing, mapping, intake, and mirror logic are mechanical and gate-tested offline against the in-memory FakeTracker, while the live Jira Cloud and Confluence Cloud connections are shipped reference implementations a repository wires to its own instance, and the round-trip is real once that live adapter is wired (explicitly: do not assume a live instance is connected the moment you install the plugin). Every module, config, field, secret reference, skill, and template the guide names exists in the shipped engine - verified against .warp/tracker.py, tracker_intake.py, tracker_mirror.py, validate.py, capabilities.yaml, plugin/skills/intake, and the two templates. No MCP claim appears anywhere in the guide.

findings.text: Non-blocking. The operator guide describes the plan epic/child mirror as part of the round-trip and correctly frames it as mechanical logic that is real once the live adapter is wired. It does not itself call out the finer edge that epic/child CREATION against live Jira is a later increment even in the reference adapter (per capabilities.yaml jira_cloud_intake_adapter: 'epic/child creation against live Jira is wired in a later increment'). This is not an over-claim: the guide explicitly warns not to assume a live instance is connected out of the box and defers the exact mechanical-versus-reference split to docs/plugin.md section 12 and .warp/capabilities.yaml, and section 12 (reviewed at WARP-0610) documents that not-yet-live edge. Recorded for the record; proportionate for a human workflow guide.

Non-blocking, out of scope, carried over from WARP-0610. The shipped plugin/templates/.warp/trackers.json uses token_ref 'secrets:jira_token' as its example, which the default resolver in .warp/tracker_intake.py (env: prefix only, else literal os.environ read) would not resolve. The WARP-0611 guide is TRUE here: it uses env:JIRA_TOKEN as its example and never claims the secrets: template value resolves. The template value is a pre-existing nit separate from this docs spec.
